rows: A raccoon has one kind of colour sensor in its eyes, and you have three. It sees brightness without hue, so the picture is grey.
A Virginia opossum also showed only one kind of cone, most sensitive to yellow-green light near 561 nanometres.
The nine-banded armadillo and the sloths have broken copies of genes that every cone needs, so they see with rods alone.
Anteaters have lost the blue-sensitive cone. The Chinese pangolin has lost it too and kept its other cone.
Raccoons, like other carnivores, have a reflecting layer behind the retina, and opossums, like many marsupials, have one within it. We brighten the shadows to suggest it.
No measurement was found for raccoons or opossums. These are our guesses.
docs/views/sheets/mammal.md#2 raccoon: Sharpness, field and pupil
The picture is grey, weighted toward yellow-green, where the opossum’s single cone is most sensitive. The weights are this app’s own.

mole.note: Mole (Talpidae): eyes under the skin; light from dark and nothing more. The same picture as the other entry.

src: docs/views/sheets/mammal.md#2 mole Light and dark: Slonaker; Animal Diversity Web

rows: An eastern mole’s eyes lie under its skin, and its eyelids almost never part enough to let light in.
Its sight goes no further than telling light from dark, so there is no picture here.
A mole finds its way and its food with a touch-sensitive patch at the tip of its nose and a keen sense of smell. Neither reaches a camera.
A grey field of light and shade is the app's way of showing light without an image. The sources give no more than light and dark.

notes.why: Rod-only eyes (armadillos, sloths) would wash out to white in bright day. A new field that compresses highlights; it waits on a source.
The black bear has a cone-dense area centralis (Heyward 2021); kangaroos may have a band. A separate bear entry would draw it once kangaroo topography is sourced.
Mole: the touch screen could light a small patch under the finger in a dark field. It would be an invention.

rows: A domestic pig has two kinds of colour sensor, most sensitive near 439 and 556 nanometres, and you have three. We show colours the way a person with only two kinds sees them.
An American black bear has a blue-sensitive cone and a red-green one, with at least three red-green cones to each blue. Sea otters carry genes for the same pair.
The tammar wallaby, a small kangaroo, has only two kinds of cone. Some other Australian marsupials have a third.
The platypus and echidnas carry genes for two kinds of cone pigment, as most mammals do.
A tammar wallaby resolves about 4.8 cycles per degree, a twelfth of your 60. A western grey kangaroo’s retina could carry about 11. We blur the picture to about 5.
Asian elephants make out a gap of 8 to 11 minutes of arc near the tip of the trunk, about a tenth of your sharpness. One African elephant managed only 48 minutes.
Bears, otters and other carnivores have a reflecting layer behind the retina that gives light a second pass. Pigs and red kangaroos have none, so the shadows are lifted only a little.
No measurement was found for these. We leave the field as your camera gives it and draw a round pupil.
docs/views/sheets/mammal.md#2 mammal: Field of view and pupil
A platypus senses weak electric fields through its bill, down to about 50 millionths of a volt across a centimetre, and can find and avoid objects by them. No phone senses this, so it is left out.
With &draw=rumble and the microphone on, low sounds shake the lower part of the picture, as vibration through the ground reaches a mole. The drawing is the app's.
